SHRI ARUN JAITLEY (Gujarat): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, the hon. Law 
Minister has moved the High Court and Supreme Court Judges (Salaries and 
Conditions of Service) Amendment Bill, 2009. Sir, I rise to support this 
Bill. And, I support this Bill primarily on the ground that in these days 
of inflation, the cost of living having gone up, salary structures, first 
in the private sector and now in the Government sector, have 
substantially changed. One of the objects in altering the salary 
structures really  is,  as  the  economy  also grows in order to give to 
all those who are the recipients of those  

 367 
salaries and service conditions, the benefit of an improved quality of 
life which they can get on those salary structures. In the case of 
Judges, when we are improving their salary structures through this 
legislation, it's also an occasion for us to ponder over the situation as 
far as the institution is concerned. I am, Sir, conscious of the fact 
that the privileges we enjoy as a Member to speak on the subject also 
requires an in-built restraint with regard to certain inter-institutional 
courtesies that various organs of the State have to maintain when they 
discuss the performance and functioning of each other. 
Sir, in this country, we function on one of the basic tenets which is 
the separation of powers. The concept of separation of powers essentially 
has conferred upon the judiciary in India the power to adjudicate 
disputes and also a very important power of judicial review is concerned. 
There has been a serious concern in the society that when all our 
institutions function, none of them tries to encroach upon the 
functioning of the other and, therefore, there occasionally has been a 
comment and suggestion when we find that the limits of activism at times 
cross the lakshman rekha. But, then, there is no division which is 
possible. The only division which is possible is by the institutions 
themselves acting in restraint and by acting in restraint, some element 
of statesmanship is also required that is fully conscious of what the 
functions of the Executive and Legislature are, the courts also take 
adequate care to make sure that they don't overstep. 
Sir, the argument is normally given to the extent that what does a 
judicial institution do at a time when other organs of the State don't 
perform their functions. And this argument has been used to support this 
contention that an overreach in such cases has to take place, otherwise, 
there would be a void as far as the constitutional set- up of the society 
is concerned. But, this argument has also certain dangers. Nobody can be 
allowed to contend that arrears are mounting up and therefore, there has 
been some inadequate performance at some levels even by our judicial 
institutions and somebody else can start performing those functions. If 
any of the organs of the State Government do not perform their functions, 
then they have to be pressed into action to perform their functions. Any 
of the other constitutional agencies do not take over the functions of 
the other organ and start performing them, and therefore, when we discuss 
the performance of our own judicial institution, this is one restraint in 

 368 
terms of statesmanship, avoidance of any form of overreach, at the same 
time, making sure that the judicial power of review is adequately 
exercised which the court will have to really bear in mind. Sir, when we 
are particularly increasing their salaries and increasing the salaries 
significantly, I consider it a welcome step, a welcome step for the 
reason that judicial offices have to be made to appear to be attractive, 
people have to be incentivised to go and get elevated and get into those 
attractive offices. If those adequate incentives are not provided, the 
best within the system will not be incentivised enough to go and occupy 
those offices, and this is already one problem which the judicial 
institution in this country is facing. We have a judicial set up which is 
broadly independent;  

 369 
we have a judicial set up which is broadly fair; we have a judicial set 
up which is powerful, but, at the same time, if we consider some of the 
problems which confront the institution, one of the serious problems is 
with regard to the quality of persons who occupy these offices. 
Historically, the best within the system were incentivised to occupy 
those offices. As the system proceeded, we have now found a situation 
where that incentive is lacking, and even from amongst members of the 
Bar, the best within the system are unwilling to get elevated. The most 
competent amongst them are unwilling to get elevated, and therefore, the 
incentive to occupy those offices is lacking, and when this incentive is 
lacking, how do we re-think about the system within which we are able to 
appoint the very best because ultimately, the quality of the institution 
will have bearing on the kind of faith people have within the system 
itself? It is extremely necessary that institutions like the judicial 
institution, institutions like the Parliament, remain objects in which 
there is a popular faith in democracy. If people start losing faith in 
the judicial institutions or in the Parliamentary system, the very 
fundamentals of our democracy get weakened, and this country cannot 
afford to fall into that sort of a situation, and therefore, we need to 
improve the system wherever we feel a problem has arisen. 
Sir, today, when I speak in terms of quality, there has been a great 
debate going on as to what the procedure of appointments should be as far 
as the judges are concerned. Conventionally, we followed a system where 
the Chief Justice of India would send his recommendations to the 
Government, and after certain element of consultation, the Government 
would decide whether to appoint them or not. But inevitably, the 
Government followed the advice of the Chief Justice. Till 1982, when this 
was crystallised and a sanction was given judicially to an opinion by a 
narrow margin of a divided court that the last word is really of 
Government, this was then re- considered and post 1993, we are now living 
in a situation where effectively in India, it is the judges who appoint 
judges. In India, it is not the President, acting through the elected 
Government, who appoints judges. They may be formally involved in some 
procedure of consultation; they may be the executive appointing 
authorities but the functions performed by the Government now in matters 

 370 
of judicial appointments have become most minimal and the predominant 
word is of the judicial institution. In 1998, we corrected it further 
through judicial pronouncement again, and it was not only the Chief 
Justice of India who is appointing the judges, but the Collegium came up. 
Now, two observations have to be made. On the basis of this Collegium 
functioning in the last 10 to 11 years, the entire process of 
consultation has become extremely slow, and while it has become slow, you 
will always find that about 25 to 30 per cent of judicial posts in the 
higher judiciary of this country, particularly at the level of the High 
Courts, are vacant. 
Each High Court would have five to seven to eight vacancies. The 
normal strength of the vacancies,  at  any  given  point  of  time,  in  
the national High Courts, taken together, is anything  

 371 
between 150 and 200. The process of consultations has become very slow. 
You know the date when a judge is going to retire. His retirement date is 
known on the date of his appointment itself, and, therefore, the 
requirement, really, is that six months before he retires, the process of 
appointing a successor should be set into motion. But, inevitably, this 
does not happen. Therefore, it is collectively that you appoint. And, one 
of the reasons why collectively you appoint is that the Collegiums, now, 
represent the collective wisdom. And because Collegiums recommend the 
collective wisdom, and too many minds go into this whole process, 
individual preferences, objective views, and also subjective views, about 
persons also get into it. The question that we have to pose and ask 
ourselves, after ten years of the Collegiums having functioned, is: have 
we been able to improve the quality of judges we are appointing in this 
country? And I have no hesitation in saying 'there is no improvement in 
the entire process of judicial appointments that we are making in this 
country!' How do we, then, improve upon the quality? That is a 
fundamental question which arises before us. To the question 'who has the 
last word', I think, earlier, the Executive had the last word; then, the 
Chief Justice of India had the last world; now, the collegium has the 
last word. The real issue has now altered from 'what was the debate', 
which has been conventionally going on, from 'who must have the last 
word', to the real issue 'as to what is the criterion on the basis of 
which you appoint judges'. Is the criterion going to be entirely 
subjective? Because the Collegium's decisions cannot be called into 
question by the Government, the Government can only refer it back once, 
and if the Collegium, again, says, "No. We insist that he be appointed", 
he would be appointed! My suggestion, therefore, is that we seriously 
reconsider, now, can we think in terms of a criterion by which the 
quality of judicial appointments can be improved? In all the systems we 
have followed till date, systematically, the quality has been coming 
down. And the quality has been coming down because subjective opinions 
about individuals have taken precedence over the objective criterion on 
which the judges must be appointed. There can well be situations where 
five judicial appointments are to be made in a high court; instead of 
appointing the best five who are available, you may pick up somebody who 
doesn't fall in the first one thousand, and it is not whether under this 

 372 
Government or under the previous Government. I am personally aware of 
cases where the selected ones are chosen, and once a person is chosen, he 
remains in office till he retires. Removal, in this country, has almost 
become unknown. And, therefore, the damage that can be done is, the 
office can either mature you; the office can also provide you immunity 
from any form of criticism. If a person with inadequate abilities is 
elevated, then he is capable of becoming even a burden on the system. So, 
my suggestion would be that the hon. Law Minister, at some stage, should 
consider a debate as to whether the discretion available to the 
Collegiums can be restricted by legislative changes. And when I say that 
the discretion available to the Collegiums must be restricted by 
legislative changes, what I, specifically,  have  in  mind  is  that  
now,  with the entire records and the functioning of our judicial  

 373 
system having become computerised, the objective details of a person who 
is considered, must be available what are his academic qualifications; 
what is the kind of experience he has at the Bar; how many cases he has 
argued and how many cases that he has argued, are, actually reported; in 
how many cases he has got the law altered or laid down. 
What is the number of youngsters that he has trained under him? What 
is his income, here is a potential available. In Government, every time 
when a number of vacancies come up there is some threshold of 
qualification. Today we have a situation before the Collegium where there 
is no threshold of qualification. If five people are to be appointed, the 
candidate on merit at No. 1000 can be chosen and appointed. It can't be 
called into question before any court. The Government can, at best, 
return it once. It can't be criticised. That is the system under which we 
function. Therefore, the real question, if we look at the declining 
quality of the appointees, as far as judicial officers are concerned, is 
that we must now seriously start a debate whether the discretion of the 
Collegium must be regulated by objective criteria with regard to the kind 
of persons that the Collegium select. Amongst the short- listed people, 
the Judges certainly are best equipped to know as to what is the 
integrity level of a candidate, how he will particularly perform as a 
Judge. Some element of discretion would always be available to them. But 
when they enter into the zone of consideration, there must be some 
threshold that they have to cross. Otherwise, I am afraid, we will not be 
able to improve the quality of judicial appointments and the quality 
can't be improved by merely altering the question. So far –  I include 
myself as part of that responsibility –  we have, in the last 25 years, 
debated the principal question: Who should appoint Judges? The real 
question is: What are the criteria on which a person is appointed as a 
Judge? I think, even under the present system, it is these criteria which 
now require to be seriously brought in. 
Secondly, when we speak in terms of improving the quality of Judges, 
the issue of accountability also is extremely important. Normally, courts 
are not criticised within our kind of system. Public debate on the 
functioning of individuals is discouraged. Contempt laws are there. 
Unless you are pushed to an extreme situation, normally, you don't bring 
out these issues for a public debate because you don't want to bring down 

 374 
the popular faith, as far as the institution is concerned. I read the 
statement of the hon. Law Minister. I think he made it yesterday. He said 
it earlier also. There is an extreme position which is the impeachment 
process. Now, the impeachment process is exercised in the rarest of the 
rare cases. It can't be utilised in every case. I do hope that such 
situations don't arise that we have to use it frequently. But then short 
of that, certain checks and safeguards are required. There are issues of 
complaints. There are other issues. After all, institutions are manned by 
men. It is not that they are always infallible. Some men are bound to 
make mistakes and let us not forget the fact that the entry into the 
judicial institution brings out a sense of fairness and sense of 
responsibility in any entrant into that institution, in a very large 
number of cases. In some cases the immunity  which  a Judge enjoys can 
actually work adversely, if his individual moorings, integrity and  

 375 
fairness are not of the best quality. Now, in such cases the Judges, so 
far, have followed an in -house mechanism in resolving these issues. The 
in-house mechanism has worked in some cases and not worked in other 
cases, and the tendency also does exist that unless pushed to an extreme 
the in-house mechanism doesn't work. Too many cases need not be brought 
into the mechanism because that will again bring a very bad name, as far 
as the institution is concerned. So, the hon. Law Minister is quite right 
when he says that the in -house mechanism is where he has not  succeeded. 
Therefore, you require some kind of an institutionalised mechanism which 
will go in these questions of serious misdemeanours when they arise. The 
extreme situation is impeachment and we have the Judges' inquiry 
legislation. But what happens in all other cases? We have an issue of the 
Punjab High Court which has been hanging fire and it has almost become a 
matter of public debate. We have another issue where some hon. Members of 
this House have submitted a memorandum to the Chairman. Do we have a  
mechanism which exists today which commands popular confidence? I humbly 
submit that such a mechanism really does not exist. I have one area of 
difference with the hon. Law Minister that when such mechanism is created 
by the legislation that he has proposed, this must essentially be a 
judge's own mechanism. If it is a mechanism of only the judge's, then the 
only change that comes about in such a mechanism is that the present 
informal mechanism which is functioning becomes a statutory mechanism. 
The structure of that does not change. It acquires a little bit of a 
statutory form. What do standards and norms of public accountability 
require? When there are serious complaints and the matter needs to be 
inquired into, can it only be left to the in- house mechanism, whether it 
is statutory or non- statutory? Therefore, some element of participation 
is required; it may be minority participation, but it has to be in the 
nature of a public participation. The law will have to be structured. The 
National Judicial Commission, which was suggested earlier, had 
predominantly a larger number of judges; the majority was judges. Then 
two of the members suggested were, one nominee of the Government; the Law 
Minister would be best suited for that purpose and the second person, an 
eminent citizen could be appointed by a Collegium comprising the Prime 
Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Speaker, Three of them 
appoint a very eminent public man who enjoys very high credibility level 
to be a party to it. It is this participation which will ensure that 

 376 
fairness is done to the person against whom the complaint has come, and 
fairness is also done in the matter of looking into the allegation of the 
complaint. Such a mechanism even from the point of view of judges will 
carry a much higher credibility level. Today, when we are having a debate 
in the House with regard to improving the quality of the judicial system, 
and this Bill which seeks to increase the salary by two- and-a-half to 
three times, in fact, it is one of the good steps in the right direction 
because it incentivises and makes the office more attractive so that the 
best talent within the system gets attracted to it. These are some 
changes and reforms which are required in this particular matter. There 
are a large number of  issues such as arrears; how the courts must  
function; what changes the Government can bring about, etc. Since they 
have been debated, I  

 377 
am not referring to them. But I have these two suggestions to make with 
regard to the appointment process and with regard to the inquiry into the 
misdemeanours. With these words, I support the Bill which the hon. 
Minister has brought as a step in the right direction. Thank you.

decided. But a proper legislation will bring about transparency in the 
matter. 
Now, the issue of encroachment is a sensitive one. The Prime Minister, 
Dr. Manmohan Singh, once said, in a polite manner, "Judiciary should not 
breach the constitutionality of demarcated boundaries." 
But the reply given by Judiciary was that they did not encroach upon 
any matter unless the Legislature failed to act. Now, Sir, if the 
Legislature fails, does any other organ of the Government have the power 
to pass or amend a law? Who has given such a power to any other organ of 
the State? I would repeat the argument which I have been making and which 
has been referred to by my colleague here; in case, tomorrow, the 
Executive says that, because thousands of judgments are pending in the 
Supreme Court and in High Courts, the Prime Minister would pass the 
orders, or, similarly, the Chief Ministers of States would say that since 
judgements were pending in the High Court and the Judiciary was not doing 
its duty, he would pass the order, what would happen? Can this logic 
survive? And if this logic cannot survive, the other logic also cannot 

 380 
survive. Therefore, each organ has to have its own restraint; they have 
to understand what their respective powers are. Today, laws are created 
more through interpretations. If you see the law that exists today in the 
form of judgments, it is much more than the laws that we have passed. It 
is ten or 20 times more. As a result, it is very difficult to comprehend 
what the law is in a given area. Therefore, this sort of increasing 
encroachment has to find some way. It is not an exaggeration, but I will 
not be surprised if a day may come when courts of law will pass order to 
the Presiding Officer of this House or the other House saying that the 
court restrains the Presiding Officer of this House or the other from 
admitting a Calling Attention Motion or a Question, or from admitting a 
discussion.  

 381 
In our rules, Sir, we have to amend or delete that rule which has 
existed for all these years. That is an anomaly. We normally say that 
matters pending in courts cannot be taken up in the form of a question, 
etc. There are many public matters which have to be discussed. But there 
is this rule which says that matters pending in courts cannot be 
discussed. So, somebody can make use of this clause and can restrain us. 
Since most of the matters which are discussed today are pending in courts 
of law, this rule should be deleted from the Statute Book to avoid any 
controversy because ultimately we will have to because of Public Interest 
Litigations. Most of the matters that we discuss are subject- matters of 
courts in some form or the other. Therefore, Sir, we have to delete that 
particular clause. Now, Sir, in order to bring transparency in the 
functioning of the Government, the Government of India has graciously 
enacted the Right to Information Act. No Department can dare to refuse 
information. Whenever information is denied, they go in appeal and the 
appellate authority decides it. A very fine and transparent procedure is 
there. Every Government department follows it. But, what about the 
Judiciary? It does not. When the Central Information Commission passed an 
order that this Act applied to Judiciary also, what has the Supreme Court 
done? The Supreme Court has challenged the order of the CIC in the Delhi 
High Court. Tell me, Sir, what would be predicam ent of the Judge or the 
Judges who decide against the Supreme Court because it is the Supreme 
Court which is the aggrieved party, which has brought it before the Delhi 
High Court saying that it is aggrieved and the CIC's order should be 
cancelled. 
Now, what is to be done by the Delhi High Court, I don't know. 
Supposing, this matter ultimately goes to the Supreme Court, either way; 
who will be deciding? The Supreme Court will be deciding. Initially, who 
was the applicant? It was the Supreme Court. Now, how is it to be 
resolved? Mr. Law Minister, Sir, you have to find some answer to it. You 
have to protect that legislation, and see to it that judges themselves do 
not decide this matter, or, you have to amend it and make a clarifying 
clause, as it is, by Parliament that it will apply, irrespective of this 
thing, to the Supreme Court also. Let it be said in clear terms, so that 
everything is resolved. Thereafter, if they will strike down the clause, 

 382 
I don't know. That is possible. Even if you put a clause that it shall 
apply to the Supreme Court, they may strike it down. That is possible. 
They are the supreme. 
Now, Sir, secondly, I would like to say that nowadays judgements are 
going against legal literacy. What I am saying is, every citizen has to 
know the law of the land, the fundamental laws. But, if you see the trend 
of the courts, they write long, long judgements, and to find out what is 
their pronouncement, it takes a lot of time. As a result, the task which 
our Law Ministry is doing today to spread legal literacy, these 
judgements go against that. The laws are to be made simple. As it is, the 
legislations which pass, sometimes are complicated. If you interpret 
judgements of thousands of pages,  it  gets  further  complicated. 
Therefore, the common citizen does not have the access to the  

 383 
knowledge in regard to what a law is. Sometimes, Sir, I feel that in the 
age of computerisation, now, whether it is possible to do it. We have to 
examine it, because if certain propositions of law are decided from time 
to time, there can be a software by which the facts of the case are put 
in the computer. The proposition of law, as decided earlier, can be put; 
and बटन दबाओ जजम�ट पाओ। In this way, the judgement can come out. Can we 
go into such a world? I mean, that is not a bad idea, Sir, because human 
discussion is going astray these days. When human discussion going 
astray, let us resort to this, Sir, that a software can be developed by 
which facts and laws are fed in the computer. Thereafter, a judgement can 
be sought from Mr. Computer on this occasion. 
Then, Sir, I am coming to a slightly different but a related matter. 
As far as the Election Commission is concerned, we have got article 324. 
During the entire period of election, everybody has experienced it now 
that there does not exist any Judiciary. Why I am saying this is because 
all the petitions related to it are to be decided after elections. There 
are so many orders which are passed by the Election Commission 
purportedly to be under article 324. They write letters day -in-day-out 
purportedly to be law, and if it violates any of my fundamental right or 
any other law, I have no remedy. The courts also give sanctity to such 
letters which are said to be judgements. They ask the Chief Electoral 
Officer to follow them. Everyday they will be writing letters now 
purportedly under article 324. Can you find some solution to this, Sir? 
It is very, very essential because those who contest elections or those 
who work or assist them become very, very helpless to get these letters, 
which are written from the Election Commission, asking them to do this 
and do that. They will just forget about the Representation of People 
Act, they will forget about the constitutional provisions, and they will 
write letters, which, according to them, is the law of the land. During 
those three weeks, nobody can do anything about it. Therefore, Sir, 
something has to be done in that context too. 
Lastly, Sir, I would like to touch a small issue relating to my State 
for the consideration of the hon. Law Minister. 
We had in Goa what is called Judicial Commissioner's Court, it was a 
High Court. That court had full powers of a High Court. Absolutely, it 
was not a bench of any court, but a full- fledged High Court. Before, we 
were under the Portuguese regime, when we had a High Court and the 

 384 
jurisdiction of our Goa High Court during the Portuguese regime extended 
overseas to other countries, to other colonies of Portugal. This was the 
status of a High Court which we had. Ultimately, when we became a State, 
we were given a bench of the Bombay High Court. We were entitled for a 
full-fledged High Court. But, we were given a bench of the neighbouring 
High Court. 
Now, technically it is a fulfilment of a Constitutional requirement. 
They club together several States and they give one. The State was 
entitled for a High Court, but a bench was given. But, the Government of 
India should now consider, after several years, the demand of Goa for a 
full-fledged High Court. 

 385 
Secondly, Sir, despite the fact that we had a strong judicia l 
background, a very good High Court, I do not know if there can be a 
State-wise representation in the Supreme Court, but I would say, Sir, Goa 
judicial officers, Goan lawyers must find a place on the bench of the 
Supreme Court of – India. It is essential,  Sir. Please consider these 
demands. Thank you. 
SHRI P.R. RAJAN (Kerala): Thank you, Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir. First 
of all, I welcome and support this Bill presented by the hon. Law 
Minister – The High Court and Supreme Court Judges (Salaries and 
Conditions of Service) Amendment Bill, 2009. I welcome and support this 
Bill because considering the hard work and the number of cases to be 
dealt with by the judges and the responsibilities that rest on them, it 
is highly and absolutely necessary to revise the salaries and allowances 
and conditions of service of the judges. It is reported that there are 
more than 50,000 cases pending in the apex court itself. So, it is highly 
necessary to appoint more judges to dispose of those cases. We must 
ensure that all citizens who approach the apex courts must be delivered 
with justice in a speedy manner. Justice delayed is justice denied. 
But, Sir, I think, I must take this opportunity to share some thoughts 
on the judicial system, especially the appointment of judges and to 
decide their service conditions. My party, the CPI(M) strongly believes 
that the Parliamentary democratic system of our country, as well as the 
executive, public and the judiciary must be given a role in appointing 
judges even in the higher courts. 
Recently, a healthy and open discussion has been initiated. It has 
been reported in the newspapers on the functioning of the judiciary. The 
Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, the Prime Minister, the Lok Sabha 
Speaker and many leading citizens of the country had taken part in this 
discussion. Sir, I would like to bring to the attention of the House that 
the CPI(M), when raised certain criticisms against the shortcomings and 
weaknesses in the functioning of the judiciary and against the approach 
of certain judgments of the Supreme Court and the High Courts, a section 
characterised the criticisms as an attack on the judicial system. 
There are reports that a section of the Judges is corrupt. The dispute 
is only about the percentage. There are allegations that some Judges are 
showing favouritism and some are insufficient. 

 386 
Sir, I would like to bring to the notice of the House a recent letter 
of the Chief Justice of India, Justice Shri K.G. Balakrishnan's, 
addressed to the Chief Justices of High Courts, and it has been widely 
reported in our media, that those Judges who do not have the 
acceptability of the trust of the people, it will be appreciable if they 
themselves leave the position as a Judge. 
Sir, judgements ignore the interests of the poorer sections and 
oppressed and restrict the efforts to ameliorate their conditions by 
social intervention. Some judgements ignore the interests of the common 
people by their complete surrender to the globalisation philosophy. 

 387 
Sir, the method of appointment of Judges is also a matter to be 
discussed. In India it is not open to public scrutiny and lacks 
accountability and transparency. Even a reasonable criticism against a 
judgement can be branded as contempt of court as per the provisions of 
the present law. Perhaps, it is only  in India that Judges are appointed 
by Judges alone. In India, till 1993, Executive had a role in the 
appointment of Judges. The nine- Judge Bench with the majority of the 
seven, by an innovative interpretation of the Constitution, took over the 
power of appointing Judges in its own hands. This came in the background 
of a weak Executive at the Centre. It held that the recommendation for 
appointment of a Judge should be made by the Chief Justice of India in 
consultation with his two senior- most colleagues and that recommendation 
should be given effect to by the hon. Present. As regards the method of 
appointing Judges by Judges itself it is a challenge to the four- pillar 
democratic system of our country. The collegium Judges who appoint the 
Judges may help in creating a coterie in future. It can also lead to the 
appointment of friends and relatives of the collegium Judges. 
The 1993 decision was reaffirmed in a unanimous opinion rendered by a 
nine-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court in 1998 on a reference made by th e 
President under article 143 of the Constitution. The method of 
appointment of Judges by Judges themselves poses challenges to the 
democratic system. The present system is incapable to appropriately 
address the diversities of India, and is not open to public scrutiny and 
lacks accountability and transparency. The system of appointment should 
be transparent and subject to public scrutiny. The public should be given 
an opportunity to express their views on the names nominated for the post 
of a Judge. 
The present law on contempt of court and the system of trial is 
inherited from the British feudal system. A common man has a right to 
approach the court against slanders and libels. In a democratic system it 
is not appropriate to give more powers to the Judges than what is open to 
a common man. The system of insulating the judiciary from public scrutiny 
and opinion with the threat of contempt of court is unjust and dangerous 
in a democratic system particularly in our country. 
The second Administrative Reforms Commission headed by Veerappa Moily 
has recommended to the Government in January 2007 to constitute a 

 388 
National Judicial Council having the representation of the executive, 
legislature and judiciary for recommending names of the judges for 
appointment and to decide their service conditions etc. of Supreme Court 
and High Court Judges for enquiry into the misconduct, for imposing 
penalties and recommending removal of judges also. My party has 
recommended the constitution of a National Judicial Commission with 
representatives from the three organs of the Government, -  Executive, 
Legislature and Judiciary -  representatives of the Bar Association and 
the general public. The Commission should be vested with powers to make 
recommendations for the appointment of judges, to conduct enquiries into 
the misbehaviour of judges,  to impose minor punishments and to recommend 
to the President for the removal of judges  

 389 
3.00 P.M. 
for misbehaviour and incapacity. Before concluding, Sir, I would request 
the House and the Government that the basic nature of democracy should be 
made applicable also to the appointment and to decide the service 
conditions and to fix the salaries of the judges also. Once again, Sir, I 
support the Bill. 
PROF P. J. KURIEN (Kerala): Sir, the independence of Judiciary is 
paramount for a healthy democracy. I support and I welcome this Bill 
which seeks to increase the salaries of judges. When the cost of living 
has gone high and the salaries of the bureaucrats have been increased 
there is adequate justification for asking such a Bill. Furthermore, as 
it has been already pointed out, there are very eminent advocates who are 
having lucrative practice and those advocates are not prepared to be 
elevated to the Bench because, for example, Mr. Ram Jethmalani is here, 
such a senior advocate, a man getting such a... 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI (Nominated): No one has ever offered me the post 
of a judge. I have not been found respectable enough. 
PROF. P. J. KURIEN: You are a luminary in that field. Even Arun 
Jaitley who was speaking here, see, so many good advocates are there but 
they do not go to the Bench. The reason is very simple. If you go to the 
Bench, the income and salary is less. You can get ten times or even 
hundred times more income by being a good advocate. So, the increase in 
salary is nominal. (Interruptions) The hon. Minister who is also a good 
advocate refused to become a judge. So, therefore, I welcome this Bill 
and I have no complaints even if judges are giving little more. Having 
said that, I have to respond to my previous speaker. I have to say that 
we have an experience in Kerala where the judiciary has come to our help 
when there are mass struggles and agitations, especially States' 
sponsored bandhs and agitations. The previous speaker, my good friend 
said that judiciary should not give judgement against mass struggles and 
mass agitations. I did not want to bring this point but because he spoke, 
I have to speak. We have in our State experience where bandhs are 
sponsored by the State, where nobody will be allowed to move even if they 
call it hartal. In effect, it will be bandhs. Pregnant mothers who want 
to go to hospitals for delivery are not allowed. 

 390 
Those who are suffering from accident or if an accident took place, 
they are not allowed. If a person is about to die of heart attack, he is 
not allowed. In every bandh, 2, 3 or 4 people die in our State. What is 
the remedy? Sir, the remedy is available only from judiciary. Our High 
Court has given a judgment that there shall not be any bandhs, because 
bandhs, especially State-sponsored... 
SHRI P. R. RAJAN: Sir, the court has not said like that. 
...(Interruptions)... 
PROF. P. J. KURIEN: If bandh is allowed, it also curtails the 
Fundamental Rights of citizens. It is my right to walk. It is my right to 
work. In our country, a few people want to undertake strike. They can do 
so. Why should they oppose others doing work? Same is the case with 
Parliament. Suppose,  

 391 
50 Members want to create problem, they can create problem by walking 
out of the House. Why should they block or interrupt the entire House? 
Therefore, judiciary has taken a welcome step by intervening and 
protecting the rights of citizens by banning bandhs and giving a verdict 
against mass agitations. The important thing is that the law has been 
upheld. The judiciary is upholding the law. So, I welcome that. Sir, 
bandhs or hartals may be either State-sponsord or whatever it is, but, at 
the same time, every citizen has a right and that right has to be 
protected. If the Government do not protect it, it is the duty of the 
judiciary to protect it. That is what I wanted to say. 
The second point is: Sir, my friend has said about the 'institutional 
courtesy.' It is correct. My friend, Shantaram Naik has already said it. 
No institution has to cross the Laxman Rekha. Neither Parliament should 
step into the realm of judiciary nor should judiciary step into the realm 
of Parliament. But, unfortunately, in certain judicial pronouncements, 
there are unnecessary interventions about the whole lot of politicians. 
If one politician is found guilty by courts, it is only one individual. 
Everyone can be a politician. To some extent, every citizen is a 
politician, because he will have something in politics. And, if a 
judicial pronouncement says, 'all politicians are barred', it amounts to 
saying that all Indians are barred. So, this kind of crossing the 
Lakshman Rekha is not correct. I don't know how it can be stopped. Let 
the hon. Minister, who is an expert in these matter, give a remedy to it. 
Sir, the next point is about judicial activism. Here also, I differ 
with my friend. My experience from what I read from newspapers and from 
others things, the judicial activism has helped the society in a number 
of cases. As has been said, 'how judicial activism helped?' I am not an 
advocate. So, I have an objective view. And, advocates have some 
subjective view. Since I am not an advocate, my view is a layman's view 
i.e., objective view. Sir, from where the judicial activism came in. No 
doubt, when the State failed, judicial activism came in. Take for 
example, Public Interest Litigation. If my memory is correct, it is 
Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer who permitted the PIL for the first time in 
Kerala. And a number of PILs have helped to correct the anomalies in the 
society and to call the Government for action. I am not saying this way 
or that way or whether it is beneficial or not. So, judicial activism, 

 392 
per se, cannot be blamed. If the Government fails, what is the remedy? 
Now, you say, judiciary can interfere and correct if the Government does 
something wrong. If the wrong doings of the Government can be corrected 
by judiciary, a question can be put to them that a failure of judiciary 
can also be corrected by the Government, because wrong doing is also a 
failure. According to my personal view, the judicial activism has helped. 
There may be a few cases in which judiciary might have overstepped. But, 
by and large, judicial activism has helped and that is what I would like 
to say. 
Then, Sir, what has been said about the process of appointment of 
judges is very correct. Judges appoint themselves! This is not good for 
democracy; this is not good even for Judiciary itself.  

 393 
Therefore, as recommended by the Law Commission, certain suggestions are 
pending here. So, I would like to request the hon. Law Minister that this 
present process of 'judges appointing themselves' should be corrected and 
necessary law should be enacted in this regard. I have even spoken to 
some of the judges, who are personal friends of mine. They also 
personally told me that they also feel that this should be corrected. A 
very senior retired judge, from Kerala, personally told me that this 
process of 'judges appointing themselves' should be corrected. So, what I 
am saying is that even judges will also agree with this. But the system 
today is allowing them; so, they are doing it. Whose duty is it to 
correct it? It is our duty. It is the duty of the Legislature to correct 
it. Therefore, I request the hon. Minister to take necessary action in 
this regard. 
Then, my friend has mentioned about an RTI case that has been referred 
to the High Court by the Supreme Court. And, he has criticised that. I 
think, by doing so, the Supreme Court has shown the best examples of 
conduct because the Supreme Court itself is a party in that. When this 
RTI case came before the Supreme Court – right or wrong, I don't want to 
say anything in this regard because I am not a legal luminary – the Chief 
Justice of the Supreme Court had taken a view. There will certainly be 
subjectivity in that. And, knowing that, the Chief Justice of India has 
left it to the High Court for judicial scrutiny and a judicial verdict. I 
think, this is one of the best examples of conduct one can show. How can 
it be criticised? Then, my friend doubts that if the Supreme Court has 
referred a matter to the High Court, what the High Court judges will do. 
They should take independent view that's why they are appointed there. If 
that question is extended — if the President makes a reference to the 
Supreme Court, can you say that because the President has made a 
reference to the Supreme Court, the Supreme Court will say what the 
President wants? Not at all. Our Judges, right from the lowest rung to 
the highest strata, are the men of character and integrity. Some of them 
may not be having integrity, they may be corrupt. But they are few. But I 
can say that most of our judges are men of character and integrity. There 
may be some corruption for which we have to take some action. But it is 
wrong to think that because the Supreme Court has referred the matter to 
the High Court the judges will be afraid of giving a judgement according 

 394 
to law and as per their conscience. I think, the Chief Justice of India 
has done a right thing by referring the matter, where he himself is a 
party, for legal scrutiny. He could have easily not referred the matter 
to the High Court and would have said that it was his own duty. But he 
did not do that. It is the highest example of democratic and judicial 
behaviour that even the Chief Justice of India is submitting his views to 
the High Court for legal scrutiny. This is what I feel. 
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: What if they give contrary judgement? 
PROF. P. J. KURIEN: As I said earlier, I am not a legal luminary. I am 
speaking as a layman. My view is also subjective. 

 395 
Then, I have to make a request to the hon. Law Minister. I have 
written to him as well as to the Chairman of the Parliamentary Standing 
Committee also regarding the number of vacancies for judges that are 
lying there. Mr. Arun Jaitley says that these vacancies are always 
pending. What is the meaning of retiring the High Court judges at the age 
of 62? 
What is the need? At 62 years, if they are incompetent, then, how can 
Ministers be there in office at 68- 70-75 years? Then, most of us will 
also be incompetent. What is the justification for this? In fact, at 62 
or 65 years of age, these judges will be more productive. When you 
appoint a judge, he is a new man. It will take 2 -3 or 4 years for him to 
understand and deliver better judgements. When the time comes for him to 
contribute and deliver really good judgements, he is retired. Such 
experienced and talented judges will be made to sit at home and you will 
give him pension also. You will have to bring a new and incompetent 
person to the Bench. What is the need for this? So, there is a strong 
need for increasing the retirement age of judges. 
Secondly, what is the need for having a difference between the 
retirement age of High Court judges and the Supreme Court judges? I don't 
understand this because in the Supreme Court, law matters and 
constitutional matters come, and interpretation of law also has to be 
done. For this you need a more alert brain. There, the retirement age is 
65 years. And in High Courts, you ask them to retire at 62 years of age. 
There is no need for having a disparity in retirement age of judges of 
High Courts and the Supreme Court. I request the hon. Minister to 
consider this. This is not just my view. The Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice has already 
recommended that this disparity should be rectified and the same has been 
recommended three times. I request the hon. Minister to seriously 
consider, approve and accept the recommendations of the Standing 
Committee. ...(Interruptions)... It should be increased and, in any case, 
both should be equal. The age- limit can be increased up to 68 years. In 
America, there are judges who are 70 and 75 years of age and they never 
retire. ...(Interruptions)... The Government has better wisdom. It can 
increase the age up to 68 or 70. The Government should decide this. It 
can increase the retirement age and, then, bring the retirement age of 

 396 
the High Court judges on a par with the Supreme Court judges. 
Lastly, I would plead for the common man; the aam aadmi of our 
country. Sir, justice is very costly in our country. It is very costly. 
Sir, ultimate justice is acquired from the Supreme Court. I don't think, 
a Keralite, unless he is a millionaire, or, a Tamilian, unless he is a 
millionaire, or, for that matter, anybody from your State, unless he is a 
millionaire ...(Interruptions)... can come to the Supreme Court and file 
a case. The expenses for coming here, meeting an advocate, fees paid to 
the advocate, etc. are very high. There are some good advocates who will 
charge less fees and argue your case. There are very few such advocates. 
A hefty fees is charged, but the common man does not,  ultimately,  get  
justice.  It  is  a  fact.  Then, what is the way out? We also want 
ultimate justice,  

 397 
whatever may be the argument on the other side. Heavens will not fall if 
a Bench of the Supreme Court is set up in the South. It could be in 
Chennai or Mangalore. Heavens will not fall if a Bench of the Supreme 
Court is set up in East Kolkata or Bhubaneswar. And, heavens will not 
fall if a Bench of the Supreme Court is set up on the Western side. This 
is needed for getting ultimate justice for the aam aadmi. Sir, I know of 
some cases where the sentence is, 'hang till death', but, the accused 
says that he is innocent. 
He cannot approach them because he does not have money. Even such 
cases are there, I know. But I do not know why our Judiciary and our 
leadership are not thinking about this. For giving ultimate justice to 
the common man, Judiciary should not be concentrated at one point. The 
Supreme Court should hold Benches in all these places. 
Sir, one more point I would like to make. In Kerala, there is an 
agitation going on. It is my duty to bring that point to the notice of 
the House. That agitation is by the lawyers of Trivandrum. They are 
asking for a bench of the High Court at Trivendrum. They are also saying 
the same thing which I have said. It is my request to the hon. Minister 
to consider both these requests favourably and take appropriate action. 
With these words, Sir, I fully support this Bill. Thank you very much.

SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: Sir, I hate to be autobiographical, but I do wish 
to share with this House that I took my legal education in the 30s and I 
started my practice in the 1941. I took my legal education in those 
colleges and under those teachers who, day in and day out, impressed upon 
us that judges discharge divine functions. 
It is the function of God to meet out justice to his creation, but, by 
the compulsion of society, we have to appoint some human beings to meet 
out justice. But, the functions, which they are essentially discharging, 
are the functions of God. Sir, I am not exaggerating, but, practically, 
all my professional life, I have devoted to supporting the dignity and 
the independence of Judges. And, Sir, look at the Constituent Assembly. 
What awesome powers did they confer upon our Judges - matters of life and 
liberty on criminal side; complete powers on the civil side, whatever be 
the property involved, whatever be the rights involved, whether it is 
ordinary property rights, or, intellectual property rights, complete sway 
over the avocations of people. But, Sir, the other power, which they 
conferred upon them was that Judges were made the guardians of the common 
man in this country. We are not merely a democracy. Our Constitution says 

 406 
that we are a Republic and a democracy. A republic is different from a 
democracy. In a democracy, the majority governs almost in every field. 
But, in a Republic, it is the individual citizen who is paramount because 
he is clothed with some inalienable rights which even the two Houses of 
Parliament acting unanimously cannot take away or abridge.  If  they  do  
abridge those rights and liberties, the abridgement has to be justified 
in the eyes 

 407 
 of our Judges who have to decide whether the restrictions are reasonable 
or not. And, Sir, what is more, the Parliament represents the will of the 
electors of India. You make a law here in both the Houses; the President 
sanctions it. But, five Judges of the Supreme Court have the right to 
turn around and tell the President and the two Houses of Parliament that 
you have passed a law, but you have passed a law without understanding 
the basic law which you enacted some 60- 70 years ago; we understand it 
better than you do, and they have the right to strike down that declared 
will of both Houses of Parliament supported by the hon. President. These 
are the awesome powers which the Constitution- makers conferred upon our 
Judges. But, they did so because they too were of the same opinion as my 
teachers that these Judges are agents of the divine power and they are 
discharging divine duties, and, Sir, look at the brilliant galaxy of 
Judges we had at that time either in the Federal Court of India or in the 
Supreme Court of India. Sir, one has to recall some of those names. I can 
say that they were Judges who could hold a candle to the best Judges in 
any part of the world. Sir, Judge like Kania Saheb, who became the first 
Chief Justice of India; Judge like Vivian Bose; Judge like Faisal Ali; in 
recent times, Justice Krishna Iyer, Justice Venkatachaliah, Justice Verma 
- these are the names to be mentioned and you get a sense of pride, you 
have a glow of pride when you think of these great Indian Judges. But, 
Sir, I agree with every speaker who has spoken before me, particularly 
with Mr. Bhatia. I do not know where he has gone now. It is unfortunate 
that standards have fallen. Standards have fallen to such an extent that 
it is, perhaps, true that on the criminal side particularly, judgements 
which were delivered 30-40 years ago by Presidency Magistrates in Madras, 
or, in Bombay, or, in Calcutta were better than the judgements which are 
now being produced in the Supreme Court. 
And, what is more, it is unfortunate that some incidents have taken 
place and evidence has surfaced which has also cast a doubt upon the 
integrity of some of the Judges, not merely at the subordinate level. 
Chief Justice Bharucha publicly declared that twenty per cent of the 
Judges in the Higher Courts are corrupt. Sir, th e people of this country 
are very anxious to know what the remaining eighty per cent of pure 
judges have done about those Judges, whom Justice Bharucha, perhaps, 
rightly described as corrupt judges. 

 408 
Sir, look at the records. A Rajasthan High Court Judge and his 
Registrar sought sexual favours from a female doctor. A committee 
appointed by the Supreme Court found them guilty. The Judge only 
resigned. The Judge should have been in jail. No further action was 
taken. Some Judges in Mysore were involved in a sexual scandal. Nothing 
serious happened. A Judge of the Delhi High Court has been formally 
charged for corrupt dealings with property developers and the trial has 
not yet commenced for more than a decade. The case raises an interesting 
question. In receiving sexual favours, does a Judge receive illegal 
gratification? It is an interesting point, which, I hope, the Supreme 
Court will have to decide. Sir, this is the state of affairs. Sir, to my 
mind, because of the very  nature  of the functions which Judges have to 
discharge, they must be completely made above  

 409 
want so that they don't have the slightest temptation, slightest envy 
with the richest persons who appear before them or whose interests and 
whose rights and obligations, they sit in judgement upon. 
Therefore, Sir, now you have trebled their salaries; for all practical 
purposes, I think, it is little less than triple. If you had made it 
quadruple or even five times, I would have still supported it. But, Sir, 
the support should come from a realisation of the great dignity of that 
judicial office and the enormous value of the functions which these 
Judges perform. 
I have a grievance against the Statement of Objects and Reasons of 
this Bill. What does the Statement of Objects and Reasons say? It does 
not talk of the great role of the Judges in our body politic. They are 
important but they are more important than even the Legislature and the 
Executive combined. They are the guardians of citizens against the 
arrogance and the corruption and the venality of power. And, Sir, this 
tribute should have been made in the Statement of Objects and Reasons.

date. I could not collect the exact date but about four years ago,

published the same year said that Indians pay out more than Rs. 20,000

with the corrupt judges which the Constitution provides, namely,

branches of our law –  criminal law, labour law, income tax law,

assistance of the Bar. So, that judge went to the commercial court, where

wanted to raise, were raised by our esteemed colleague, Shri Ram 
Jethmalani. However, I would like to make a few points. At the outset, I 
appreciate the intention behind the Bill. Our judges must have comforts, 
their material living conditions must improve and there must not be any 
compromise on that score. Having said that, I must point out that the 
system in which we live today with the Constitution which is a republican 
one, the Parliament, the Judiciary and the Executive have certain defined 
roles, and they are very important components of our democracy. But very 
often we find that there are conflicts from time to time between the 
Parliament and the Judiciary, and I think, here, the Parliament which 
represents the will of the people, must be treated as the supreme since 
the Parliament makes laws, the Parliament represents the will of the 
people and the conflicts between the Parliament and the Judiciary must be 
sorted out appropriately, and in any way, the Judiciary should not 
encroach upon the rights and positions of the Parliament. The other 
problem is that justice must be given to people on time. Justice delayed 
is justice denied. In a way, justice hurried is also justice buried. But 
we find today in the Indian prisons, thousands of people who are kept in 
prolonged confinement, prolonged detention for petty crimes or for no 
crimes at all because they are not being tried, they are not being 

 416

prolonged confinement, prolonged detention leads them to further crimes

poorer sections of the society. They are not from the hi- fi section of 
the society. If you go to any central prison, the number of prisoners who

the poorer sections of the society. This is where the Judiciary must be 
more humane and must be more concerned to deal with these people.

society. Here, I think, the judicial reforms become imperative. Now, it 
is high time that we went in for judicial reforms. There, I agree with 
many of the previous speakers; we should seriously think of constituting 
a National Judicial Commission. These judicial reforms must be 
implemented and judicial accountability must be established. Here comes 
the question of disclosure of assets by Judges. Can Judges disclose their 
assets or not? I do not know why it has become a debatable point. What is 
wrong in the Judges disclosing their assets? There was a seminar, held in 
New Delhi, by the Bar Association. 
Our respected Ram Jethmalani was saying that the Bar must be involved 
in the constitution of the National Judicial Commission. There was a 
seminar. Many legal luminaries were sitting there. I said, "I am a 
layman. I am asking: What is wrong in the Judges declaring their assets?" 
Then everybody said, "What is wrong in the Judges declaring their 
assets?" Why should it be an issue of debate? Why should it be an issue 
of controversy? Why shouldn't the Judges declare their assets? If a 

 420 
Member of Parliament has to declare his assets, he has to file an 
affidavit. Then, why shouldn't a Judge? We are not asking for something 
which we should not ask for. If you increase the salaries of Judges, we 
have no problem. Yes, they must be given enough salaries and their 
comforts are very important. But why shouldn't they declare their assets? 
What is the way out? How are you going to do it, as a Government, as the 
Law Minister? Are they above all these things? At least, that must be 
explained to the common people because finally it is the common people 
who are the guarantee for any justice. They are the guarantee for any 
democracy. They are the guarantee for any functions of the bureaucracy. 
If people don't have confidence in the judiciary, then the judiciary 
can't perform. You can say that they are performing the duties of divine 
power. But when people don't have confidence  in  the  judiciary, where 
is the question of discharging the duties of divine power? That is  

 421 
where, I think, the judiciary must rise above all pernicious, biased and 
parochial tendencies. Our country is diverse in nature. It is a very 
complex country. There is a unity of different cultures and social 
milieus. If the judiciary does not reflect and understand this, we will 
get into troubles. That is why people demand that there must be proper 
representation of different sections of the society in the judiciary. 
There are also parties in India which demand reservation in the judiciary 
also because they think judiciary is biased. So, it is time that we 
restored the integrity of the judiciary. It is time that we restored the 
confidence of the people in the judiciary for which the Government and 
we, as Members of Parliament, will have to do certain things. I think, 
when a conflict between the judiciary and the Parliament arises, the 
Parliament must have the supremacy to settle the issue. The Parliament 
has the will of the people to make laws and the judiciary is there to 
uphold the laws and to see to it that the law is implemented. With these 
words, I conclude.

three minutes. 
SHRI B. S. GNANADESIKAN (Tamil Nadu): I will finish within three

Coming to the points raised by my friend, Shri Raja, he spoke of the

things.

SHRI D. RAJA: That was my view. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P. J. KURIEN): That is your view, I know. I

SHRI B.S. GNANADESIKAN: There is a proverb by Prof. Bernard Shaw. It 
says, "The freedom of your walking stick stops where my nose begins". The 
Supreme Court wanted to protect my nose  

 423 
only. When you wanted to wave the stick, the Supreme Court and the high

Now I come to PIL. There are many issues like minimum wages,

Sir, I would like to make two points so far as this Bill is concerned.

The second point is in regard to the LTC. Sir, only three LTCs are
